183.title: A lamp to my feet (Psalm 118 [119]:105)
183.hook: thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths
183.carry: enough light for the next step
183.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 118 [119], this verse included, in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some say verse 105 before reading scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alphabet psalm, aleph to tav: twenty-two stanzas, one for every Hebrew letter. Your line was a to z of love. Today, that long psalm opens at a single verse.

You get up in the night for a glass of water. The house is dark. You don't turn on every light. You tap your phone's flashlight and point it at the floor. It shows about three steps: the edge of the rug, the corner of the table, the doorway. And it's enough. You don't need to see the kitchen from the bedroom, only the next step, and then the one after that. Long before flashlights, a psalmist had the same thought.
screen: `A DARK HOUSE AT NIGHT.` → `A LIGHT FOR THREE STEPS.` → `AND IT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: The verse sits in the middle of yesterday's alphabet psalm, at the start of the stanza for the letter nun. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." First, picture the lamp. Not a streetlight or a lighthouse. In ancient Israel a lamp was a small clay dish with olive oil and a wick; the Hebrew word is ner. Hold one up at night and it lights a small circle around your feet. That's the point: the psalmist isn't promising a floodlight over the whole road. God's word lights the next step. Second, what it doesn't promise. It doesn't say you'll see the map, or know where the road bends next year. It's tempting to want the whole route before starting out. The psalm offers something smaller and steadier: enough light to walk by. Third, why that can be a comfort and not a letdown. A small light has to be carried close. In the psalm, the walker keeps near the word, one step at a time. Catholics hear God's word here in two senses: the scriptures they read, and the Word made flesh, Christ, whom Saint John calls the light. Jews hear it as the Torah, the teaching that guides daily life. Both read the same verse and hear the same promise: not everything, just enough.

segments.voice: Think of the next thing you'll walk into today: a room, a meeting, a hard conversation, a school gate. Don't plan the whole day; just see the doorway. If you pray, say the verse slowly, thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths; if you don't, ask yourself what the next right step is, only the next one.

184.title: Songs of the road (Psalm 120 [121])
184.hook: pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem sang these: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains
184.howItsDone: Catholics pray the gradual psalms (Psalms 119–133 [120–134]) in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hour, and Psalm 120 [121] is sometimes prayed for travelers and at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ner, the small clay lamp. Your line was enough light for the next step. Today, the road itself.

Two hours into a long family car trip, somebody starts a song, everybody knows the words, and the miles go faster. Now take away the car. Families walking for days toward Jerusalem for the great feasts: grandparents, kids, neighbors from the same village. The last stretch is uphill all the way, because Jerusalem sits high in the hills. And as they climbed, they sang. The Psalter kept their road songs, fifteen of them in a row.
screen: `A SONG ON A LONG TRIP.` → `FAMILIES WALKING TO JERUSALEM.` → `UPHILL, SINGING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Fifteen psalms in a row carry the same heading. In Hebrew it's shir ha-ma'alot, a song of the goings up. The Latin Bible made it canticum graduum, a song of the steps, so the Douay-Rheims calls each one a gradual canticle. Gradual here has nothing to do with slowly; it comes from the Latin gradus, a step. Other English Bibles call them the Songs of Ascents. Second, the steps. Nobody knows for certain why they got the name. Some readers think it's the climb up to Jerusalem. An old Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, says the Levites sang on fifteen steps in the Temple, one song for each step. Either way, these are songs for people on the move, going up. Third, today's psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." A pilgrim looks up at the hills, a long climb ahead. Where does help come from? Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the promise: "Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel." On the road you sleep in the open, and someone has to keep watch. The psalm says someone is. Catholics still pray the gradual psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and this one is sometimes prayed for travelers, and at funerals, for the last journey.

segments.voice: Look up at something high, a tree, a rooftop, a hill, the ceiling, the sky through a window, and let your eyes rest there while you name the climb in front of you this week. If you pray, say the line: my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. If you don't, just stay with the looking up, and let your shoulders drop.

185.title: I rejoiced (Psalm 121 [122])
185.hook: let us go into the house of the Lord; pray for the peace of Jerusalem
185.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 121 [122] in the Liturgy of the Hours, often at Vespers on feasts of Mary, and its first verse, Laetatus sum, is the psalm verse of the Latin entrance chant for the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gradual psalms, songs for the climb to Jerusalem. Your line was help comes. Today, the pilgrims arrive.

Let's go. Let's go to the beach. Let's go see Grandma. Let's go to the game. Two words, and before anyone has moved an inch, the trip has begun. Today's psalm starts right there. Somebody in the village says, we're going up to the house of the Lord, and the psalmist's heart jumps. A few lines later, the pilgrims are standing inside the gates of the city they walked for days to reach.
screen: `LET'S GO.` → `THE HEART JUMPS.` → `STANDING INSIDE THE GATES.`

segments.voice: It's one of the gradual psalms, a road song, and it opens with joy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." First, the joy. Nobody is forcing anybody here; going to worship is the good news, the thing to look forward to. Its first line is the psalm verse of the old Latin entrance chant for Laetare Sunday, the Sunday of rejoicing in the middle of Lent, and it's used in the Liturgy of the Hours for feasts of Mary, who is sometimes called the house of God. Second, the arrival. The pilgrims stand inside the gates and look around at a city built close together, where the tribes go up to praise the name of the Lord. A long road, and now: here. Third, the prayer. The psalm turns and asks for peace: "Pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem: and abundance for them that love thee. Let peace be in thy strength: and abundance in thy towers." The Hebrew says it more plainly: peace within thy walls. And there's a play on sounds. Peace is shalom, Jerusalem is Yerushalayim, and the lines chime shalom, shalom, as if the city's own name held the word. Tradition has long heard it that way, though scholars aren't sure that's where the name comes from. Today Jerusalem is holy to Jews, to Christians and to Muslims, and people of all three pray for its peace. The psalm doesn't say whose peace. It asks for peace inside the walls, and for the ones who love the city.

segments.voice: Picture Jerusalem: stone walls, narrow streets, people of three faiths walking past each other every morning, and hold the ones there who are grieving or afraid. If you pray, say the psalm's line, pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem; if you don't, wish peace to the people who live there, and then to one home you know where peace is thin.
I rejoiced. The first words of a pilgrim psalm: glad to be invited into the house of the Lord, and praying for the city's peace. Today's word.
Your line: peace within thy walls. A long road, and then the gates. That's one hundred eighty-five days.

186.title: Unless the Lord build (Psalm 126 [127])
186.hook: they labor in vain that build without him
186.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 126 [127] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some begin the day with a morning offering, a traditional prayer that offers the day's work, joys and sufferings to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I rejoiced: pilgrims inside Jerusalem's gates, praying for its peace. Your line was peace within thy walls. Today, another road song, this one about work.

It's eleven at night. The laptop is still open. One more email, one more fix, one more thing, and you tell yourself if you push a little longer, it'll all hold together. The coffee's cold. Tomorrow you'll get up early and do it again. It's the loop where everything seems to rest on one person, and stopping for a second feels like letting it all fall down. Long ago, someone wrote a psalm for exactly that person.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, STILL WORKING.` → `IT ALL DEPENDS ON ME.` → `A PSALM FOR THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: Another of the gradual psalms, and the heading gives it to Solomon, the king who built the Temple. It opens with two pictures. In the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." First, what it doesn't say. It doesn't say don't build, or fire the watchman. The builder still lays bricks; the guard still stands on the wall. The psalm is about who the work finally rests on. Second, the tired worker. The next verse calls it vain to rise before light, eating the bread of sorrow. Then a line of real gentleness: "When he shall give sleep to his beloved." In the psalm, rest isn't laziness. It's trust: the house isn't held up by one pair of hands. Third, the house. In Hebrew, house can mean a building and also a family, a household, a line of children. So the psalm goes on to children as a gift from the Lord. Build a home, raise a family, run a city: the psalm says all of it rests on God first. The Latin opening, Nisi Dominus, was set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi, and it's carved as a motto over doors and on city arms. Catholics also have an old habit that fits it well: the morning offering, a prayer at the start of the day that hands over all the day's work before it begins.
screen: `TWO PICTURES: BUILDER AND WATCHMAN.` · `STILL BUILD. STILL WATCH.` · `SLEEP TO HIS BELOVED.` · `HOUSE MEANS FAMILY TOO.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Name the main thing you'll work on today, a project, a shift, homework, looking after someone, and see yourself starting it. If you pray, hand it over: this is yours, Lord, before it's mine; some Catholics use the morning offering for this. If you don't pray, set an intention: I'll do my part, and I won't carry the whole house alone.

187.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 129 [130])
187.hook: the psalm prayed for the dead
187.howItsDone: Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, in the Office of the Dead, at funerals and gravesides, and especially in November; it is also prayed at Night Prayer on Wednesdays in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nisi Dominus, unless the Lord build. Your line was not in vain. Today is a quieter psalm. Go gently.

Some nights you're not on the road anymore. You're at the bottom of something. A diagnosis. A funeral. A mistake you can't take back. A phone call at three in the morning. Words run out, and you can't manage anything polished or brave. Down there, people have reached for the same short psalm for well over two thousand years. Monks sang it at evening prayer. Families say it at gravesides. A famous writer's letter from prison was published under its first two Latin words.
screen: `AT THE BOTTOM OF SOMETHING.` → `WORDS RUN OUT.` → `ONE SHORT PSALM.`

segments.voice: It opens at the lowest point. In the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." In Latin, De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine. First, the depths. In the Bible the deep waters are chaos and drowning, the place where your feet can't touch. The psalmist is in over his head, and he says so. The prayer doesn't wait until he's feeling better; it starts from the bottom. Second, the turn. Next he speaks of sin, disarmingly honest: "If thou, O Lord, wilt mark iniquities: Lord, who shall stand it." If God kept a ledger, nobody would last. Then the hinge: with God there is forgiveness. That's why this is one of the seven penitential psalms. Third, the waiting. The psalm doesn't end with rescue. It ends with hope that keeps going around the clock: "My soul hath hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch even until night, let Israel hope in the Lord." The Hebrew pictures a watchman on the wall, waiting for dawn. Anyone who has sat up with someone sick knows that watch, waiting for the window to go gray. Fourth, the dead. Because it cries from the depths and hopes for mercy, the Church took this psalm as its prayer for those who have died. It's sung in the Office of the Dead, and for centuries Catholics have prayed the De profundis for the souls of the faithful departed, often at graves, often in the evening. Catholics believe the prayers of the living can help the dead on their way to God.
screen: `STARTING FROM THE BOTTOM.` · `IF YOU KEPT A LEDGER, WHO COULD STAND?` · `WAITING FOR THE MORNING.` · `THE CHURCH'S PSALM FOR THE DEAD.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Let one person who has died come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to. Remember one ordinary thing about them, the way they laughed, what they always cooked. If you pray, pray the psalm's first line for them, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord; if you don't, keep a quiet minute in their memory.
De profundis. Latin for out of the depths: the first words of the psalm the Church prays for the dead. Today's word.
Your line: my soul hath hoped. Even from the depths, the watchman waits for morning. Until tomorrow.

188.title: Like a weaned child (Psalm 130 [131])
188.hook: three verses about a quieted soul that doesn't grasp at great things
188.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 130 [131] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it for quiet prayer, repeating its short verses slowly as a way of resting in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, De profundis: the cry from the depths, prayed for the dead. Your line was my soul hath hoped. Today, the psalm right after it, and it's very quiet.

Watch a hungry baby for thirty seconds. Everything is wanting: crying, reaching, grabbing at the one thing that will make it better, right now. Then watch a toddler a year or two later, on a parent's lap after a long day. Not grabbing. Not asking for anything. Just leaning back, heavy and content, because being held is enough. Two very different ways to be a child. And a psalm only three verses long says a soul can learn the second one.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY: ALL WANTING.` → `A TODDLER ON A LAP: CONTENT.` → `A SOUL CAN LEARN THAT.`

segments.voice: It's another gradual psalm, headed as David's, and it starts by letting go of ambition. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, my heart is not exalted: nor are my eyes lofty. Neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me." First, who's talking. The heading gives it to a king, somebody with every reason to grasp at great things, and he says: I've stopped. I don't need to understand everything or run everything. Second, the picture. The Douay follows the Latin: "As a child that is weaned is towards his mother, so reward in my soul." The Hebrew is plainer: I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother. Weaned is the key, and the Hebrew word is gamul. A mother in the Second Book of Maccabees reminds her son that she "gave thee suck three years." A nursing baby on its mother's lap wants one thing and cries until it gets it. A weaned child can sit on the same lap and want nothing but the closeness. So this isn't a soul that feels nothing. It's a soul that has stopped demanding, content to be held. Third, the mother. The psalm names only a child and its mother, but some readers hear God in the mother's place, with the psalmist resting on her lap. Saint Thérèse's little way, which we met back in the saints, breathes the same air. Then the psalm turns to the whole people: "Let Israel hope in the Lord, from henceforth now and for ever."

segments.voice: Settle into your chair, let it take your full weight, and let your hands open in your lap. Notice what you're reaching for, the answer, the outcome, the thing you want to happen, and for two minutes, don't reach. If you pray, rest in God the way a child rests on a parent's lap, wanting nothing but to be there; if you don't, rest in being held up by the chair and the floor.

189.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136 [137])
189.hook: exiles weep, and the last verse is raw rage; the Church keeps it honest, not as a command
189.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 136 [137] in the Liturgy of the Hours without its final verses, and read the whole psalm in scripture as the lament of the exiles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gamul, like a weaned child: a soul content to be held. Your line was quieted. Today the quiet breaks. This one is raw.

There's a reggae song with these words, and later a dance-floor hit. Bright, bouncy, easy to sing along to. The words come from a psalm, and the psalm is no party. It's exiles sitting beside foreign rivers, far from home. Their city has been burned. Their Temple is gone. And the people who carried them off stand over them and say: go on, sing us one of the songs of Sion.
screen: `A SONG FROM THE RADIO.` → `EXILES BY FOREIGN RIVERS.` → `SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF SION.`

segments.voice: First, the history. The Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and carried many of its people away to Babylon. This psalm is their voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." They hang their instruments on the willows. Then the taunt comes, and their answer: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Second, the vow. If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, the psalmist says, let my right hand be forgotten. Jews have kept that vow close; one explanation given for the glass broken at a Jewish wedding is to remember Jerusalem even in the middle of joy. Third, the ending, and it's hard to hear. The last verse blesses whoever would take Babylon's little ones and dash them against the rock. There's no softening it. It's the voice of people who watched their own city fall. So what does the Church do with it? It doesn't pretend the verse isn't there. It keeps it in the Bible as an honest cry, not a command. The psalmist doesn't act on it; he says it to God. In the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church leaves those last verses out of common prayer. And some of the old monks read them another way: Saint Benedict, in his Rule, speaks of dashing evil thoughts against Christ, the rock, while they're still small. That's the surprise here: the Bible lets people bring even their worst anger into prayer.

segments.voice: Notice one thing you're angry about, something done to you, or to someone you love, or something in the news, and name it plainly in your head without dressing it up. If you pray, hand it to God as it is, rough and unfinished, the way the psalmist did. If you don't, let yourself feel it without acting on it, and breathe out slowly.
Sion. The Douay's name for Jerusalem, remembered by exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon, in a psalm whose last verse is rage handed over to God. Today's word.

Your line: even anger can be prayed. The week ran from a lamp to the feet, up the pilgrim road, into Jerusalem's gates, out of the depths, to a quiet lap, and now to the rivers of exile. See you tomorrow.
